" **28;29352;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1728115 " /&gt; &lt;h3&gt;Five roads to Lhasa&lt;/h3&gt; &lt;p&gt; Lhasa de Sela left a small but near-flawless body of work . All three of her studio albums &amp;mdash ; 1997&amp;rsquo ; s La Llorona , 2003&amp;rsquo ; s The Living Road and 2009&amp;rsquo ; s Lhasa &amp;mdash ; are recommended unreservedly , so picking a highlight from each is an exercise in pure subjectivity . Still , here are three suggestions , along with a pair to represent two areas in which her art also thrived : collaborations and live performances . &lt;/p&gt; **31;29382;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; The alchemy achieved by de Sela and Yves Desrosiers on her career-making debut album is nowhere better demonstrated than on this rhythmically eccentric song co-written with her father , its portmanteau title meaning the flower ( flor ) and the song ( canto ) . The stop-and-start arrangement complements a vocal of remarkable empathy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 640 " height= " 480 " src= " https : **33;29415;TOOLONG ... frameborder= " 0 " allow= " accelerometer ; autoplay ; encrypted-media ; gyroscope ; picture-in-picture " **34;29450;TOOLONG &lt;h3&gt;La Frontera&lt;/h3&gt; &lt;p&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s an irony illustrative of de Sela&amp;rsquo ; s gifts as an enabling musical synthesist that one of the most Mexican songs in her catalogue should feature as its lead instrument the trumpet of Lebanese-French musician Ibrahim Maalouf , whose Middle Eastern stylings fit into the ranchera arrangement perfectly . Meanwhile , de Sela demonstrates a poet&amp;rsquo ; s knack for blending the metaphysical and the prosaic . At a time when certain world leaders are putting up new barriers , a song like this is invaluable . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 640 " height= " 360 " src= " https : **34;29486;TOOLONG ... frameborder= " 0 " allow= " accelerometer ; autoplay ; encrypted-media ; gyroscope ; picture-in-picture " **34;29522;TOOLONG &lt;h3&gt;That Leaving Feeling&lt;/h3&gt; &lt;p&gt; De Sela&amp;rsquo ; s friendship with Stuart A. Staples , leader of the cult English band Tindersticks , led to three collaborations : two with the group proper and this gem from 2006 , when she joined him on his solo album Leaving Songs . An exquisite duet on a song whose theme of restlessness and romantic misgiving could have been tailor-made for her . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 640 " height= " 480 " src= " https : **34;29558;TOOLONG ... frameborder= " 0 " allow= " accelerometer ; autoplay ; encrypted-media ; gyroscope ; picture-in-picture " **34;29594;TOOLONG &lt;h3&gt;Who by Fire&lt;/h3&gt; &lt;p&gt; Many Leonard Cohen songs have been covered by many , many people . " data-portal-copyright= " ANNEGRET HILSE " **28;30179;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1727771 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; BERLIN &amp;mdash ; Philippe Falardeau was still processing the scale of what he was living , Thursday afternoon . The Quebec director&amp;rsquo ; s latest film My Salinger Year was about to officially launch the 70th Berlinale &amp;mdash ; a.k.a. the Berlin International Film Festival &amp;mdash ; on Thursday evening . And a lot of fuss was being made . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s a big spotlight for a small film , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; That&amp;rsquo ; s how I feel . But I couldn&amp;rsquo ; t refuse this moment . Part of me wants it to be over , and part of me is saying : &amp;lsquo ; Slow down , because this won&amp;rsquo ; t happen again . You have to understand what&amp;rsquo ; s happening and experience it , accompany your actors and not wish that the brouhaha ends here . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And brouhaha there was . At the jam-packed press conference after the mid-day press screening of the film , Sigourney Weaver received the royal treatment , and became the focus of most of the questions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Weaver is not the star of the film &amp;mdash ; or at least she&amp;rsquo ; s not supposed to be . But star power is impossible to repress . Her supporting turn as a veteran tough-nosed New York literary agent is delightfully scene-stealing. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But rising star Margaret Qualley holds her own portraying Joanna Rakoff , the real-life writer on whose memoir the film is based . Rakoff spent a year working as a secretary for J.D. Salinger&amp;rsquo ; s literary agent in the &amp;rsquo ; 90s . Qualley brings quirk and charisma to the part of a young woman searching for her voice . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Because despite the enticing title , this movie isn&amp;rsquo ; t really about Salinger at all . He appears intermittently at the other end of the phone line , which Joanna answers with friendly enthusiasm , if not awe &amp;mdash ; she had never read anything by Salinger when she got the job . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nor had Falardeau when he began making his movie . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Salinger for me , was a really relevant writer that I hadn&amp;rsquo ; t read , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; ( Joanna ) takes a while to read Salinger , so I put myself in her shoes . I knew of Salinger , his importance and aura . But I wrote my first draft ( of the script ) without reading him . Then when I read him , I had an epiphany , as Joanna did in real life &amp;mdash ; but I did it at 49. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Most people read him when they&amp;rsquo ; re young , in their adolescence . I didn&amp;rsquo ; t expect to like it , but I liked it very much , probably more than I would have in my teens . It was a revelation . After that , I made sure this was not a film about Salinger , but about the effect of a writer on a young woman , and her journey to becoming a writer . " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;30727;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1724275 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Expressions of love , be it revenge in the wake of love gone sour , love in a world of eccentricity , singles in search of soulmates or the unmitigated love of a child for his mother , are coming to the Hudson Village Theatre , beginning in April . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Each of the four plays in Hudson Village Theatre&amp;rsquo ; s 2020 professional season looks at love through a distinct lens . Single tickets and multi-play passes are on sale now . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Artistic director Dean Patrick Fleming has expanded the season by one production this year , allowing him to select plays to launch and close the series that reach beyond the pure fun of conventional summer stock theatre . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; First up is Leni Parker in The Blonde , The Brunette and the Vengeful Redhead ( April 16-26 ) . Parker was in the HVT production of Marion Bridge last summer . Fleming directs the one-woman , murder-mystery-comedy by Australian playwright Robert Hewett. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This one looks at what happens when you love a bit too hard , &amp;rdquo ; Fleming said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Parker plays seven characters through eight monologues , ranging from a preschool boy to a 45-year-old man to a 90-year-old woman . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The story unravels , bit by bit , as we meet the people who were in the ( murdered person&amp;rsquo ; s ) life , &amp;rdquo ; Fleming said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The season closes with another solo show , Duncan Macmillan&amp;rsquo ; s Every Brilliant Thing ( Oct. 22-Nov. 1 ) . Daniel Brochu stars and Fleming directs . Brochu was in the HVT production of Art in 2018. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Brochu plays a fellow who , as a seven-year-old , creates a list of things to love about life to give to his mother , who suffers from depression and has attempted suicide . As he grows older , the list grows longer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s one of the best things I&amp;rsquo ; ve ever read , &amp;rdquo ; Fleming said . &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s scary , but fantastic . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The play unfolds within a reconfigured performance space , with audience members sitting onstage as well as front of house . This accommodates interaction between Brochu and members of the audience . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt;A season book-ended by two solo productions with demanding narratives. &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When you are dealing with one actor , the level of trust has to be huge , &amp;rdquo ; Fleming said . &amp;ldquo ; That&amp;rsquo ; s why I chose Leni and Daniel . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Multi-award-winning theatre director Micheline Chevrier comes to Hudson to direct Pulitzer Prize-winning American playwright John Patrick Shanley&amp;rsquo ; s Outside Mullingar , starring Brian Dooley , Pauline Little and Kathleen Stavert ( July 3-19 ) . Dooley was in the HVT production of The Drawer Boy in 2019. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Outside Mullingar tells the tale of an introverted farmer and his spinster neighbour who yearns to capture not only his attention , but his love . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s a quirky , romantic notion of what rural Ireland is like , written by a New Yorker , &amp;rdquo ; Fleming said . &amp;ldquo ; Shanley has always been one of my favourite playwrights. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Shanley won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama for Doubt : A Parable and an Oscar for Best Original Screenplay for the movie Moonstruck. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Strawberries in January is by Governor General Award-winning playwright &amp;Eacute ; velyne de la Cheneli&amp;egrave ; re and translated by GG-winner Morwyn Brebner ( Aug. 6-23 ) . It traces the stories of four Montreal singles in search of love . Fleming directs Quincy Armorer , Lucinda Davis , Mike Payette and Warona Stshwaelo . Fleming said the play stands apart because of its almost cinematic structure . Told through a series of flashbacks , he said it&amp;rsquo ; s as if &amp;ldquo ; two plays are happening at the same time . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt;This season will be the first for Fleming as a bonafide Hudsonite . Then he joined the military and was sent to Afghanistan . He returned from the brutal tour with PTSD . At first he hid his symptoms , feeling isolated and ashamed , until a colleague twigged to the panic attacks and urged Carey to seek help . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As his therapy moved forward , Carey turned to music , and soon playing guitar and writing songs took a prominent place on his journey toward better mental health . He wanted to help others discover the healing nature of music , so he began to teach guitar to &lt;a href= " https : **33;31397;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;veterans at the Ste-Anne Hospital&lt;/a&gt; in Ste-Anne-de-Bellevue , as part of the Guitar for Vets program . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Carey wrote songs about combat , pain and anger , and then dug deep into his surplus of courage to perform at open-mic nights and &lt;a href= " https : **33;31432;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;at the last Hudson Porchfest&lt;/a&gt; . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt;At the urging of a fellow vet , Carey is taking his music one big step farther , with an evening of original and cover songs , called Coming Home to You : What It 's Like to Go to War , at the Royal Montreal Regiment , Saturday . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;div id= " fb-root " &gt;&lt;/div&gt; &lt;script async= " 1 " defer= " 1 " crossorigin= " anonymous " src= " https : **33;31467;TOOLONG ... class= " fb-video " data-href= " https : **28;31502;TOOLONG ... data-width= " 640 " &gt;&lt;blockquote cite= " https : **33;31532;TOOLONG ... class= " fb-xfbml-parse-ignore " &gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;31567;TOOLONG ... " data-portal-copyright= " Christinne Muschi " **28;32880;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1724082 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; American chart topper and streaming sensation Post Malone&amp;rsquo ; s headlining Bell Centre set on Sunday night aspired to be a rock show in rap clothing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In front of a rowdy , youthful crowd emboldened by his calls for drunken revelry and clamouring for some of radio&amp;rsquo ; s stickiest , most insidious hooks , Malone emulated his favourite emo and rock frontmen with his mic-stand-straddling mannerisms and throaty wails . But the musical backdrop was pure pop-trap anatomically built to shatter Spotify records , and the resulting combination proved too irresistible for most in the audience , even as the patterns became overly familiar during the 90-minute set . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Malone , dressed casually in a white t-shirt and jeans , flied solo on a thin catwalk , only accompanied by a backing track . He opened with the title track from 2019 album Hollywood&amp;rsquo ; s Bleeding , which pairs a hip hop beat with melancholic guitar . It&amp;rsquo ; s a prevalent mix both on the album and this current tour , but with the low-end still reigning in the mix , the increased use of guitar felt like more of an aesthetic decision than a left turn toward rock &amp;lsquo ; n&amp;rsquo ; roll . Malone was likely a keen pupil of the rapcore scene of the late &amp;rsquo ; 90s/early &amp;rsquo ; 00s , but while those bands were rockers at heart with some rap flourishes thrown in , Malone was born in the era of rap and sees rock as something to reverse engineer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Where Malone has always identified more as a rocker , besides his affinity for emo posturing and frat boy arrested development , is in attitude/antics ( as he states in less graceful terms on Rockstar ) . On Sunday , he described his songs to the crowd as being about &amp;ldquo ; feeling like s*** and having your heart broken , &amp;rdquo ; and one got the sense that even though he&amp;rsquo ; s using hip hop tools and expressions , Malone&amp;rsquo ; s key to success in the mainstream has been plugging in to tried and true suburban angst of his favourite rock heroes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; After Better Now from 2018&amp;rsquo ; s Beerbongs and Bentleys and Saint-Tropez early on in the set demonstrated his melodic chops and ability to rap and sing in equal measure , Malone took stylistic chances with the punk pop and cheerleader-influenced Allergic and cartoon bubbly rap of Candy Paint , but the subtleties of both got lost in the omnipresent bass . That was followed by Psycho , one of Malone&amp;rsquo ; s signature tunes with an obvious singalong element the crowd enthusiastically telegraphed . Wow from Hollywood&amp;rsquo ; s Bleeding was pure pop rap . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Malone was joined virtually by an all-too-brief video cameo from Ozzy Osbourne , who guested on the album track Take What You Want . Inspired by the guitar solo that ends the song and that also appeared here in pre-recorded form , Malone delivered a heavy metal scream with gusto and donned an acoustic guitar for Stay . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I can&amp;rsquo ; t play guitar like the solo on the last song , but can I play some guitar ? &amp;rdquo ; Malone asked the audience before admitting in Malonian fashion that he played a ton of beer pong prior the show . He returned to a guitar sample &amp;mdash ; a dead ringer for Broken Social Scene or America , depending on your age &amp;mdash ; for the &amp;rsquo ; 70s soft rock ode Circles , his most realized rap-rock hybrid yet . After his earliest hit White Iverson and Spider-Man soundtrack cut Sunflower , Malone smashed his acoustic guitar and doused it with Bud Light at the conclusion of the aforementioned Rockstar. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He concluded the night with Congratulations from 2016 breakthrough album Stoney , and while it remains one of his most memorable hooks , after 90 minutes of Malone returning to the same vocal flows again and again , as catchy as they were , one ended the evening wishing for a little more spontaneity . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;32910;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;32952;TOOLONG ... flash reaction turns Post Malone into **25;32987;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;33014;TOOLONG ... But deep in the woods , no one can hear you scream . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That&amp;rsquo ; s because all verbal communication is forbidden during the five-day silent retreat that is the setting for the play . It&amp;rsquo ; s presided over by the amplified voice of the unseen Teacher ( Marcelo Arroyo ) , who makes up for the silence with amusingly platitudinous parables and asinine observations about cold medicines and his own boring dreams . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Much of the fun lies in watching the reactions of his clients , a motley sextet who sit in a row of chairs dutifully taking notes or squirming in silent rebellion . When class is dismissed , they go off to wordlessly squabble in their spartan cabins or get into scrapes in the surrounding nature . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There&amp;rsquo ; s something Chekhovian about Bruno-Pierre Houle&amp;rsquo ; s gorgeous set design , with its expanse of wooden decking and autumnal trees . But it&amp;rsquo ; s Tolstoy&amp;rsquo ; s famous quote about families that comes to mind as we watch these seekers of enlightenment all being unhappy in their own way . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Joan ( Alison Darcy ) and Judy ( Warona Setshwaelo ) are a couple whose relationship is buckling under the strain of an illness . More immediately , one of them is less convinced than the other by all the New Agey trippiness. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Rodney ( Gabe Grey ) is a celebrity yoga teacher with a misplaced confidence in his own mindfulness . Alicia ( Zara Jestadt ) is a minor actress struggling with a breakup , panic attacks and an un-Zen-like tendency to make as much noise as possible . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the play&amp;rsquo ; s wordiest section , Ned , one of life&amp;rsquo ; s losers , hits the microphone and lists all the disasters that have befallen him . It&amp;rsquo ; s a very funny monologue with an existentially terrifying payoff and is beautifully delivered by Matthew Gagnon with a hangdog shrug . Jan ( Andreas Apergis ) , the most enigmatic character , turns out to have perhaps the most tragic backstory . He also has a double-whammy of climactic twists , by turns delightfully funny and achingly sad . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Even the teacher , who receives most of Wohl&amp;rsquo ; s satirical barbs , is ultimately drawn with a generosity of spirit , paying tribute to his sincere solicitousness for his clients and his agonized doubts over whether he&amp;rsquo ; s doing them any good . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Despite the temptation for silent knockabout comedy , the humour is mostly gentle . Director Caitlin Murphy and her cast keep things nicely focused and the characters clearly drawn ( though a couple of moments of over-compensatory mugging threaten to break the spell ) . Clarity is added by the discriminating shifts of Martin Sirois&amp;rsquo ; s lighting and by Sophie El Assaad&amp;rsquo ; s subtly inventive costume design . Rob Denton&amp;rsquo ; s evocative natural soundscape and serene incidental music manage to stop the silences from getting too awkward . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At a brisk , interval-less 90 minutes , it&amp;rsquo ; s a quietly entertaining evening . But I did wonder if it could have risked a more contemplative pace now and then , if only to immerse us in that silence , and the play&amp;rsquo ; s themes , all the more deeply . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Small Mouth Sounds plays to March 1 at the Segal Studio Theatre , 5170 C ? te-Ste-Catherine-Rd . So it&amp;rsquo ; s with great enthusiasm that an array of Canadian filmmakers will descend on the &amp;uuml ; ber-hip German cultural hub , and Quebec is leading the way . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Philippe Falardeau was stunned to learn his latest feature , My Salinger Year , had been chosen as the Berlinale&amp;rsquo ; s opening film . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It felt a bit unreal , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; I didn&amp;rsquo ; t quite understand what it meant . Sometimes opening films can be a bit tricky . At the Cannes Film Festival , they&amp;rsquo ; re often big commercial films and it&amp;rsquo ; s more about who&amp;rsquo ; s going to be there and who is willing to pay for the opening party . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; But at Berlin , it&amp;rsquo ; s a different thing . I&amp;rsquo ; m just starting to grasp what it means for the film . ArtsLocal NewsMontreal moviesNewsMcCord Museum 's graceful Griffintown photographs find logic amid chaoshttp : **35;35951;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;35988;TOOLONG ... title= " " My photographs are like puzzles that you have to figure out , with lots of spatial ambiguities , " says Robert Walker . " alt= " " My photographs are like puzzles that you have to figure out , with lots of spatial ambiguities , " says Robert Walker . " data-portal-copyright= " Pierre Obendrauf " **28;36023;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1721759 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;36053;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Robert Walker grew up in Hochelaga-Maisonneuve . As the crow flies , that 's not terribly far from Griffintown . But for the boy who was to become one of Montreal 's best-known photographers , the working-class/industrial district to the southwest -- the very place that forms the subject of the McCord Museum 's new one-man show Griffintown : Evolving Montreal -- may as well have been a different world . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; " My mother would say , ' Never go there . It 's too dangerous , full of crazy drunken Irishmen , ' " said the son of Scottish immigrants , recalling his childhood in the 1940s and ' 50s . " Anyway , in those days people did n't get around much . You stuck to your own neighbourhood . You stayed on the block . " &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Fascinated from an early age by cameras , Walker obtained a degree in visual arts from Sir George Williams University , where a pivotal experience was a workshop given by the celebrated American photographer Lee Friedlander . Walker was awakened to the richness and artistic potential of street photography , a form in which he soon broke from the prevailing tradition by choosing to use colour . His work came to international notice via a series of studies of Times Square . Made while living in New York , they demonstrate a flair for what he calls " finding a logic and a rationale in a very chaotic setting . " &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;It 's a knack demonstrated to great effect in the McCord show , where 20 large-format prints and a slide show of a further 100 shots impose a counterintuitively graceful form on a district that might strike passersby as a case study in urban development run amok . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;36089;TOOLONG ... title= " Griffintown : Evolving Montreal is on display at the McCord Museum through August . " alt= " Griffintown : Evolving Montreal is on display at the McCord Museum through August . " data-portal-copyright= " Pierre Obendrauf " **28;36124;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1721757 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Little more than a square kilometre in size , and with fewer and fewer visible vestiges of its past , Griffintown presented Walker with special challenges when he was asked to photograph it for the first instalment of the McCord 's planned Evolving Montreal series . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; " I was a little bit apprehensive as to whether I 'd find enough subject matter there , " he said . " I assumed it would be a desolate area of boarded-up buildings and warehouses . But when I got down there it turned out to be fantastic , with all kinds of construction and demolition , very interesting contrasts between the 19th century -- the Lachine Canal and the old ( cal ? che ) horse stables -- and the 21st. " &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;What strikes the viewer time and again is how Walker 's lens fixes on the things one might normally be tempted to skip over in the search for something more conventionally picturesque : piles of rubble , construction fences , partially obscured machinery looming like malevolent agents of destruction , occasional glimpses of the distant downtown skyline and the mountain providing contrast . It 's a powerful demonstration of the maxim that photography is less about what you shoot than it is about how you frame it , and Walker has a master 's eye . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;36154;TOOLONG ... title= " Robert Walker was initially apprehensive when asked to photograph Griffintown for the McCord Museum , " but when I got down there it turned out to be fantastic , with all kinds of construction and demolition , very interesting contrasts between the 19th century ... and the 21st. " " alt= " Robert Walker was initially apprehensive when asked to photograph Griffintown for the McCord Museum , " but when I got down there it turned out to be fantastic , with all kinds of construction and demolition , very interesting contrasts between the 19th century ... and the 21st. " " data-portal-copyright= " Pierre Obendrauf " **28;36189;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1721755 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Working only on clear , sunny days , the better to bring out his subjects ' inherent hues ( " If the colour does n't work , then to me it 's not really a photograph , more just a snapshot " ) , Walker also takes an evident delight in investing his images with layer upon layer of texture and contrast , all of it achieved not through trickery but with a sure sense of composition . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; " My photographs are like puzzles that you have to figure out , with lots of spatial ambiguities , " he said . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;It 's borne out in every photograph from the show , with some even incorporating a touch of trompe l'oeil , as when an image of people lounging by a rooftop pool turns out , on closer inspection , to be part of a billboard advertising a condo development yet to be built . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; " That 's an idealistic depiction of a scene that , let 's face it , will probably never happen , " Walker said . " I enjoyed showing it alongside what really is happening . " &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;36219;TOOLONG ... title= " Robert Walker 's powerful images of piles of rubble , construction fences and partially obscured machinery in Griffintown demonstrate the maxim that photography is less about what you shoot than it is about how you frame it . " alt= " Robert Walker 's powerful images of piles of rubble , construction fences and partially obscured machinery in Griffintown demonstrate the maxim that photography is less about what you shoot than it is about how you frame it . " data-portal-copyright= " Robert Walker " **28;36254;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1721758 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;If a touch of social protest might be discerned from that last statement , and from the show in general , Walker claimed it 's not overt -- saying , for example , that he does n't especially regret the loss of swaths of the district 's architectural heritage . What he does regret is what 's replacing it . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; " ( Griffintown ) was never all that interesting architecturally . The buildings were pretty banal . But what 's going up now is totally antiseptic -- condo buildings that will never see a ray of sunlight , one unit facing directly onto somebody else 's . Parking is impossible . You never seem to see any children . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; " The universities have these urban planning departments -- well , where are they when you need them ? " data-portal-copyright= " Allen McInnis " **28;37050;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1718222 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Over a relic of a cash register in what passes for the garage office , there is a photo of Henriquez at 17 , next to a Fiat and Mini Cooper that he raced in Chile . He had won his share of trophies as a teen and was told he might have been able to make it on the racing circuit . But he felt he didn&amp;rsquo ; t have the right kind of temperament . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; My idea of a great time in a car is taking my Model T for a ride in the summer , &amp;rdquo ; he says with a broad smile , &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And the only kind of ticket he might nab in his Model T would be one for going too slow . He kids that it could take him a week to go from 0 to 90 kilometres an hour . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This is one chill dude , even when delicately picking apart engines of cars in for service . His son , Juan Guillermo , or Juan Jr. , shares his dad&amp;rsquo ; s passion for collecting &amp;mdash ; in his case old toys and comic books &amp;mdash ; and for cars . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; How could I not love antiques ? I&amp;rsquo ; ve been surrounded by them all my life , &amp;rdquo ; Juan Jr. , 34 , says . &amp;ldquo ; But I have to be careful when swinging tools , so I don&amp;rsquo ; t knock out some 300-year-old piece . Or spill oil near the old Montreal Forum seats or the &lt;a href= " https : **33;37080;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;sweaters of Jean B ? liveau&lt;/a&gt; and Sidney Crosby , even though they&amp;rsquo ; re glass-protected. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;37115;TOOLONG ... title= " Gas masks , pilots ' helmets , old telephones and other military gear are on display at Garage Henriquez in the Point . " alt= " Gas masks , pilots ' helmets , old telephones and other military gear are on display at Garage Henriquez in the Point . " data-portal-copyright= " Allen McInnis " **28;37150;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1718223 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I love when people come here for the first time . Many are so confused and ask if this is a garage or antique shop . So I tell them that it&amp;rsquo ; s both . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; But I don&amp;rsquo ; t sell anything here , &amp;rdquo ; Juan Sr. quickly interjects . &amp;ldquo ; This is not about me making money from this . This is my passion . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Adds the grinning Juan Jr. : &amp;ldquo ; That&amp;rsquo ; s for sure . It&amp;rsquo ; s about passion not profits for my father . But you really have to respect that . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Juan Sr. is a Renaissance man in a mechanic&amp;rsquo ; s smock . His words come out almost like poetry . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; My satisfaction comes from seeing the eyes of kids and their parents growing wider with such amazement as they wander through here , &amp;rdquo ; Juan Sr. rhapsodizes. &amp;ldquo ; Still , it&amp;rsquo ; s also nice when they want to have work done on their cars . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Longtime customer Patsy Aguilera concedes that she rarely , if ever , hung out in garage service areas before coming here . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This is so impressive , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; ve never seen anything like it . I sometimes think I bring my car in more just to look around . There&amp;rsquo ; s always something new , actually old . But don&amp;rsquo ; t forget these are also very good and honest mechanics , which can be very hard to find . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In a tiny room , in another corner , Juan Sr. points out &amp;mdash ; no , not his tools , still don&amp;rsquo ; t know where he hides those &amp;mdash ; a mini-Coca-Cola vending-machine museum , including a motor-less one that goes back about 80 years and requires constant ice packed in the bottom . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; My mother also loves this stuff , otherwise she never could have lasted all these years with my father , &amp;rdquo ; Juan Jr . jokes . &amp;ldquo ; Still , I&amp;rsquo ; m sure she&amp;rsquo ; s happier he keeps it here and not at their home , otherwise she would never be able to find her way out . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But Juan Jr . believes his dad&amp;rsquo ; s ultimate motivation here is to keep history alive . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; These days people don&amp;rsquo ; t repair stuff , &amp;rdquo ; Juan Jr . says . &amp;ldquo ; They replace everything from phones to cars . In his own small way , my father just wants to remind people of some of what mankind has created over the centuries , before this stuff is lost and forever forgotten . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And that he has , although hardly in a small way . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **32;37180;TOOLONG " **39;37214;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " http : **28;37255;TOOLONG " target= " blank " rel= " noopener " **30;37285;TOOLONG &; ... &lt;/p&gt; Bill Brownstein , Montreal GazetteMon , 10 Feb 2020 17:59:09 **45;37317;TOOLONG ... " data-portal-copyright= " Dario Ayala " **28;37433;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1714706 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Billy Georgette&amp;rsquo ; s final concert was on the 14th floor of the Montreal General Hospital in mid-January . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He played a few songs on an old , badly-out-of-tune piano and by the end of the little gig , doctors and nurses came out of their offices to give him a warm round of applause . Four days later , he was dead . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The veteran Montreal jazz musician learned he had lung cancer in December and it spread throughout his body . He died on Jan. 21 at the age of 85. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; He played the piano four days before he died , &amp;rdquo ; his sister , Susan Georgette , said in a phone interview . &amp;ldquo ; There was a piano on the 14th floor and I had an orderly help me . We put him in the wheelchair and we wheeled him down ( from the 15th floor where his bed was ) . And the doctors told me , &amp;lsquo ; It hasn&amp;rsquo ; t been tuned in 100 years . &amp;rsquo ; The night before I went , because I can play piano , and I played some chords and it was terribly untuned. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We brought Billy down there and , my God . He first played one of his own compositions , a classical piece , and then he played They Say It&amp;rsquo ; s Wonderful , and then he played a bebop tune . You would not believe how it sounded . It was not out of tune . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; His touch was always so beautiful . And it came through on that piano . And when I looked down that hall , everyone had come out of their rooms , and all the people were just listening . And when I wheeled him out , the whole floor clapped as we walked by . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Susan was crying as she finished recounting the experience . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Her brother was a fixture in the jazz clubs and hotel bars of the city for several decades , starting in the early &amp;rsquo ; 60s playing with bands at Rockhead&amp;rsquo ; s Paradise , the legendary jazz venue at the corner of St-Antoine and Mountain Sts . He would often be the only white musician on stage playing with African-American musicians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Here&amp;rsquo ; s what the late , great Montreal Gazette columnist Nick Auf der Maur wrote about Georgette in 1986 : &amp;ldquo ; &lt;span class= " doctext " &gt;&lt;span class= " dochighlight " &gt;Billy Georgette&lt;/span&gt; is the epitome of the old trouper. &lt;/span&gt; If you&amp;rsquo ; re not a jazz fan , perhaps you haven&amp;rsquo ; t heard of him . But chances are , if you&amp;rsquo ; ve walked into a hotel or a bar in the Montreal area at some point in the past 30-odd years and heard a piano playing , you&amp;rsquo ; ve seen &lt;span class= " dochighlight " &gt;Billy Georgette&lt;/span&gt; performing . It could be said he&amp;rsquo ; s the dean of Montreal club piano players . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He used to play piano at the old Hotel de la Montagne and Moby Dick&amp;rsquo ; s bars in the 1980s and in more recent years was a regular player at the downtown venue/restaurant House of Jazz ( formerly Biddle&amp;rsquo ; s ) . He played with jazz greats like Mel Torm&amp;eacute ; and Spike Jones , with pop stars like Gordon Lightfoot and Joni Mitchell , and Quebec singers Pauline Julien and Patsy Gallant . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Georgette was part of the cool bohemian scene on Mountain , Drummond and Stanley Sts. in the late &amp;rsquo ; 50s and early &amp;rsquo ; 60s , playing at places like the Little Vienna jazz caf&amp;eacute ; . Susan tells the story of the time at the Little Vienna a young Leonard Cohen came up to her brother and asked if he could read some poetry while Georgette and his band played a little bebop . Georgette said &amp;lsquo ; yes&amp;rsquo ; and he and Cohen became good friends . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the late &amp;rsquo ; 90s , he formed a group called The Paradise Band along with bass player Errol Walters , drummer Andy Shorter and tenor saxophonist Richard Parris . They started the band and came up with the name when they realized during a conversation at Biddle&amp;rsquo ; s they all had played at Rockhead&amp;rsquo ; s at one time or another . They released an album in 1999 , titled Paradise Band , in tribute to the legendary jazz watering hole . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;37463;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " http : **34;37505;TOOLONG ... He was very well-known . He was really THE source for information about jazz here . If people had to write about Montreal jazz , they&amp;rsquo ; d come see him . He also knew a lot about the history of hockey . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Georgette did extensive research into the history of hockey and the Stanley Cup , eventually writing a musical , Victoria Rink : Le Hockey Enchant&amp;eacute ; , the title referring to the downtown Montreal rink that was reportedly the venue for the first-ever ice-hockey game in 1875. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Georgette was one of the founders of the Society for International Hockey Research and he fought for years to make Montreal the centre of the hockey universe . He wrote an opinion piece for the Gazette in 2002 making the case for building a museum park near the Bell Centre , with a rink for kids , a giant hockey stick and the world&amp;rsquo ; s largest puck . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Billy Georgette is survived by his wife , Marthe Joncas ; his three sons , Zebulon Perron , Willo Perron and Matt Labush ; and his two sisters , Susan Georgette and Linda Paquet . Mozart&amp;rsquo ; s Great Mass in C Minor and Jacques H&amp;eacute ; tu&amp;rsquo ; s Symphony No. 5 , if you want to know the particulars . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Well , no kidding . A Yannick sellout in the Maison symphonique is about as hard to predict as a full house in the Bell Centre for the deciding game of a ( quite hypothetical ) Canadiens-Bruins playoff series . Yannick is more than the local boy made good . He is &lt;a href= " https : **33;38010;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;the Montreal maestro gone international&lt;/a&gt; . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Yet there is another crowd count , one that invites quiet admiration . &lt;a href= " https : **33;38045;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;Kent Nagano&lt;/a&gt; and the OSM sold 92 per cent of available seats to a January Schubert festival that packed six concerts into six days . That would be more than 11,000 tickets . Not many cities can support a sustained outflow of serious symphonic repertoire in a month when potential ticket-buyers are gasping at their credit-card expenses . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The big Schubert turnout was not due to a special fascination with this composer . Nagano-led concerts on Feb. 18 and 20 ( Beethoven&amp;rsquo ; s Symphony No. 6 &amp;ldquo ; Pastoral&amp;rdquo ; and a newly commissioned Symphony for Organ and Orchestra by the hardcore French modernist&amp;nbsp ; Pascal Dusapin ) are also sold out . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The audience is increasing every year , &amp;rdquo ; says OSM chief executive Madeleine Careau. &amp;ldquo ; Not 100,000 people every year , but one , two per cent . It&amp;rsquo ; s quite encouraging for us , especially considering that the cultural offering in Montreal is so wide , so huge . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It is remarkable also given &lt;a href= " https : **33;38080;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;the long-term directorship of Nagano&lt;/a&gt; , which comes to an end , after 14 years , in August . Apparently Montrealers have not yet tired of the charismatic American . Schubert&amp;rsquo ; s Symphony No. 1 was rewarded with applause between movements , a sure sign that he still attracts newcomers . How the OSM will fare next season , when the throne is vacant , is a pressing question . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;38115;TOOLONG ... title= " Kent Nagano acknowledges the crowd at the start of the OSM 's free outdoor performance of Verdi 's Requiem at Olympic Park in August 2019. " alt= " Kent Nagano acknowledges the crowd at the start of the OSM 's free outdoor performance of Verdi 's Requiem at Olympic Park in August 2019. " data-portal-copyright= " Christinne Muschi " **28;38150;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1715996 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Numbers are encouraging also at the OM , according to that orchestra&amp;rsquo ; s CEO , Jean Dupr&amp;eacute ; , who reports a 20 per cent increase in subscriptions over the last five years . He identifies the European tour of late 2017 as a breakthrough in consciousness-raising , although N&amp;eacute ; zet-S&amp;eacute ; guin , the native son who &lt;a href= " https : **33;38180;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;in September was made artistic director for life&lt;/a&gt; , has been leading the official opposition since he was appointed in 2000. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; More and more people are aware of the OM and what it is , what our culture is , how we present things , how different we are , &amp;rdquo ; Dupr&amp;eacute ; said last week , citing the case of a Yannick-led outdoor concert in July that drew an estimated 35,000 onlookers to the foot of Mount Royal . &amp;ldquo ; I think we are attracting Montrealers. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Similar multitudes converge on the outdoor OSM extravaganzas supervised by Nagano every August at Olympic Park . It is hard to believe that the picnickers who flock to such events differ significantly in their symphonic allegiances. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 640 " height= " 360 " src= " https : **33;38215;TOOLONG ... frameborder= " 0 " allow= " accelerometer ; autoplay ; encrypted-media ; gyroscope ; picture-in-picture " **34;38250;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; In the Maison symphonique there might be some distinctions , although neither orchestra has recently made any systematic study of its consumer base . Dupr&amp;eacute ; , who makes a point of attending at least one OSM concert a year &amp;mdash ; &amp;ldquo ; I don&amp;rsquo ; t tell anybody , but I do&amp;rdquo ; &amp;mdash ; sees a few general trends . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In terms of age , it&amp;rsquo ; s a little bit younger , &amp;rdquo ; he says of the OM crowd , compared to the OSM. &amp;ldquo ; There are more families . People dress differently . &amp;rdquo ; That probably goes double for the outreach concerts in the boroughs and suburbs on which the OM has prided itself for decades . &amp;ldquo ; We are not a static orchestra , &amp;rdquo ; Dupr&amp;eacute ; adds . &amp;ldquo ; We are dynamic and moving . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some critics have judged the OM audience in the Maison symphonique to be quieter and more attentive , an opinion that is hard to reconcile with the public rebuke delivered by YNS to a restless Maison symphonique crowd in November . As for the OSM , there are certainly plenty of veteran concertgoers who suppress&amp;nbsp ; their coughs and leave their cellphones in their pockets , but Nagano&amp;rsquo ; s mysterious drawing power creates a&amp;nbsp ; heterogeneous mix . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;38286;TOOLONG ... title= " Yannick N ? zet-S ? guin is more than the local boy made good . He is the Montreal maestro gone international . " alt= " Yannick N ? zet-S ? guin is more than the local boy made good . He is the Montreal maestro gone international . " data-portal-copyright= " Allen McInnis " **28;38321;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1716000 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The question of language is vexed . Ten years ago , this author wrote a column upbraiding anglos who &amp;ldquo ; don&amp;rsquo ; t know from Yannick. &amp;rdquo ; That was then . It would take a strange species of ostrich in 2020 not to be aware that &lt;a href= " https : **33;38351;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;the music director of the Philadelphia Orchestra and the Metropolitan Opera lives in Montreal&lt;/a&gt; . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It is tempting , but inadvisable , to resort to stereotypes . Perhaps the OM is young in orchestra years , but it is hardly a new ensemble , having been founded in 1981 by Conservatoire students who regarded the Orchestre symphonique de Montr&amp;eacute ; al ( which sported an alternative legal name , Montreal Symphony Orchestra , from 1954 to 1979 ) as a closed shop substantially populated by English-speaking musicians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Of course , Charles Dutoit&amp;rsquo ; s mother tongue was French , but the ultra-efficient Swiss toggled between languages in rehearsal according to the musicians being addressed or what lingo got the point across quicker . If this reality conflicted with the OSM&amp;rsquo ; s storied aptitude for French repertoire , so be it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; French was more clearly entrenched at the OM . The artistic directors following Marc B&amp;eacute ; langer &amp;mdash ; Agnes Grossmann and Joseph Rescigno &amp;mdash ; while not native French speakers , were quick studies . The arrival of N&amp;eacute ; zet-S&amp;eacute ; guin in 2000 left no doubt of the primary language of rehearsal , although OM players would be expected to work in English with guest conductors , notably as the usual pit band for the Op&amp;eacute ; ra de Montr&amp;eacute ; al . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; No law prevents a music lover &amp;mdash ; French-speaking , English-speaking or Tagalog-speaking &amp;mdash ; from enjoying concerts by either orchestra . David Hutchinson , a retired software analyst , went so far as to subscribe to both before giving up on the OSM , partly as a protest against its withdrawal a few years ago of the seniors&amp;rsquo ; discount , which , as a boomer , he was looking forward to . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I like their underdog status &amp;mdash ; say , Concordia versus McGill &amp;mdash ; and the price was right , &amp;rdquo ; Hutchinson wrote in an email about the OM . The OSM was relying too much on &amp;ldquo ; gimmicky&amp;rdquo ; programming ( the OSM website at the moment is flogging &lt;a href= " https : **33;38386;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;a pair of Music , Fashion and Movement concerts&lt;/a&gt; featuring the input of the couturi&amp;egrave ; re Marie Saint Pierre ) . Hutchinson also welcomes the OM emphasis in 2019-20 on female guest conductors . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Still , the consensus is that anglos are more likely to attend the OSM. &amp;ldquo ; I think this is a matter of history more than a matter of their having had the chance to be exposed to the OM , &amp;rdquo ; Dupr&amp;eacute ; says , while essentially confirming the hypothesis . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Careau prefers to stress the multicultural character of the OSM crowd . &amp;ldquo ; We still have anglophones , but we also have allophones , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; For the past 15 years , maybe 20 , we have had a lot of immigrants , mostly speaking French , which is a world language . And the children of the anglophones are more French-speaking . They go to school in French . They are universal citizens . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Online and print communications from both orchestras are fastidiously bilingual , but it is noteworthy that OSM pops programming is now geared mostly to francophone listeners . The 2019-20 season opened officially on Sept. 17 with Nagano leading Shostakovich&amp;rsquo ; s Symphony No. 13 ( &amp;ldquo ; Babi Yar&amp;rdquo ; ) , but there were three concerts the previous week featuring the chanteuse Diane Dufresne. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;38421;TOOLONG ... title= " While the OSM throne will be vacant next season following the departure of Kent Nagano , chief executive Madeleine Careau believes the orchestra will survive the interregnum . " I am really confident about the programming . I have no doubt about this . " " alt= " While the OSM throne will be vacant next season following the departure of Kent Nagano , chief executive Madeleine Careau believes the orchestra will survive the interregnum . " I am really confident about the programming . I have no doubt about this . " " data-portal-copyright= " Allen McInnis " **28;38456;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1715995 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; If not quite apples and oranges , the ensembles are distinct varieties of apple . The OSM is a salaried orchestra with 92 permanent positions ( about a dozen of which are temporarily vacant ) . The 2019-20 minimum is $1,955 per week for a 46-week season ( for a total of $89,930 ) . Titled players , of which there are many , make more than the minimum . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The OM is a per-service orchestra with 58 musicians on its roster ( who are joined by extras in larger repertoire ) . There is a guaranteed minimum amount of work , which Dupr&amp;eacute ; says the orchestra inevitably surpasses by 50 per cent . Musicians are paid at a rate of $173.34 per service for OM presentations and the standard Guilde des musiciens rate for other events , for a typical annual total of about $32,000 . Many members of both orchestras work as teachers , the OSM players often at McGill and the OM players at the Universit&amp;eacute ; de Montr&amp;eacute ; al or the Conservatoire . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The OSM , with a 2018-19 budget of $37 million , has not only a bigger payroll but more tickets to sell . The OM ( with a 2018-19 budget of $7.1 million ) offers 16 events in the Maison symphonique in 2019-20 , including two concert performances of Beethoven&amp;rsquo ; s Fidelio in October that were co-produced by the Op&amp;eacute ; ra de Montr&amp;eacute ; al . The OSM has booked a dozen Maison symphonique concerts ( not counting recitals ) in February alone . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The elder orchestra deploys a wider variety of programming , including recitals and concerts involving the Grand Orgue Pierre-B&amp;eacute ; ique . Happily for purists , the language problem limits OSM involvement in the Hollywood blockbuster business &amp;mdash ; the Toronto Symphony Orchestra in May offers its followers four opportunities to see Star Wars : The Force Awakens with live accompaniment &lt;em&gt; -- &lt;/em&gt; &amp;nbsp ; but leaves open the cinematic high road ( next month , Chaplin&amp;rsquo ; s silent classic&amp;nbsp ; The Gold Rush , with titles in English and French ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In some respects , the OM&amp;rsquo ; s underdog image affords it a PR advantage . Nagano led the OSM on a tour of the Americas in October , including two concerts at the famous Teatro Col&amp;oacute ; n in Buenos Aires , but Yannick and the OM got all the love in November for the orchestra&amp;rsquo ; s first performance in Carnegie Hall . " We will offer EVs from every brand , every segment , every body style , every price point @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The automaker displayed 10 new and updated EV models at the event on Wednesday , including the Cadillac Lyriq luxury SUV and the GMC Hummer EV , both of which will be formally revealed to the public this spring . The electric Hummer will be manufactured at GM 's retooled Detroit-Hamtramck assembly plant , which is currently undergoing a $2.2 billion conversion to become GM 's first all-electric assembly facility . <p> A new version of the Bolt EV , launching in late 2020 , was also on display at the event , as well as the 2022 Bolt EUV -- the long-rumored crossover version of GM 's all-electric car -- which is set to launch in the summer of 2021 . <h> Ultium batteries <p> At the center of GM 's amped-up EV strategy is a new modular propulsion system architecture powered by the company 's proprietary Ultium batteries . This third-generation platform will support GM 's entire EV lineup going forward , with the flexibility to power a wide range of trucks , SUVs , crossovers , cars and commercial vehicles . <p> The Lyriq and the electric @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ third-generation EV platform and Ultium batteries . <p> " This is a huge opportunity for us , " said GM President Mark Reuss of the new EV strategy . " It represents a chance to reinvent the company and reset our brands . It will change this company and people 's perception of it forever . " <p> GM says the strength of the system starts with the battery cell , which uses state-of-the-art " NMCA " chemistry . These cells cut cobalt content by 70 percent by increasing the use of nickel and adding aluminum . <p> As part of GM 's broader EV strategy , the company plans to sustainably source as much of its battery materials content as possible from North America , and it will build the cells in collaboration with LG Chem in Lordstown , Ohio . GM first announced its plans to build the $2.3 billion battery plant in late 2019 . According to GM , this design allows engineers to optimize battery energy storage and layout for a wide variety of vehicle models . But if you 're looking for the most thought-provoking view in the state , skip the beaches and mountains , and head for Bakersfield 's Panorama Park . <p> When you walk through this narrow neighborhood park atop the Panorama Bluffs on Bakersfield 's northern edge , you do n't actually see everything . It only seems like you can . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Country , you are not just looking out upon our nation 's greatest valley . You 're also witnessing how California 's past and present are converging to create a different future . <p> The view also provides undeniable evidence that in California , you really can defy the laws of chemistry : oil and water mix here , perhaps too well . <p> The water appears first . The Kern River meanders below the park 's bluffs , amidst willows , cottonwoods and sycamores . This pastoral river can feel like an oasis amidst the larger , drier landscape . But it 's also a portal into the past . <p> The landscape you see from Panorama Park used to be one of California 's wetter places , with rivers and lakes . In heavy rains or heavy snowmelt in the Sierras , the middle of California would become an inland sea . <p> But beginning in the 19th century , farmers tamed those volatile river and lake waters , eventually creating today 's drier landscape . Dams and canals went in . From Panorama Park , you can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Canal . Water supplying the Carrier Canal also feeds the Kern Island Canal -- Bakersfield once had so much water around it that its name was Kern Island . <p> Bakersfield is still an island -- perhaps California 's largest isle -- in politics and culture . It 's a redoubt of reactionary Republicanism in a blue state , and an oil economy surrounded by the more agricultural San Joaquin Valley . <p> The vista from Panorama Park demonstrates this . Beyond the river , oil fields stretch north , further than your eye can see . The stretches of oil derricks , like the trees in Sequoia National Park , are so vast that they do n't fit the human field of vision , and ca n't be easily photographed . <p> Kern River Oil Field helped turn California into America 's leading oil producer in the early 20th century . It brought people from around the world , to work and live here . From Panorama Park you can see Oildale , where Merle Haggard grew up in a box car , and wrote a song about it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as the Bakersfield Sound . Poor people , successors to the Haggards , still live out there , and still pay too much for sub-standard housing . <p> The Kern River Oil Field has produced 2 billion barrels and counting . But its output has fallen dramatically since 1985 ; production has been propped up by pushing steam into the wells to draw out the sticky remaining oil . This is a costly practice , both economically and environmentally , and support for the oil business is not bottomless , even here . A court recently ordered Kern County to halt new oil permits . From Panorama Park , you 're looking at an industry in decline . <p> Bakersfield is changing in other ways , too . If you stand in the park and turn away from river and the oilfields , you 'll see Alta Vista-La Cresta , one of the city 's older neighborhoods . The Alta Vista tract was first laid out by Donald McClaren , son of John McClaren , who put together @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a distinguished address -- its denizens had those grand views -- but the area has been fading ever since Bakersfield expanded west of Highway 99 , and richer people bought places in neighborhoods like Seven Oaks . <p> The Panorama Vista -- specifically , the area between the bluffs and the oil fields to the north -- has been the focus of successful restoration for more than a generation . It 's been called the Panorama Vista Preserve since 2004 , and visitors there enjoy trails and a native plant nursery . <p> It 's not hard to imagine the preserve growing larger , and the vista changing . As California responds to climate change , the state will turn harder against oil . @@84046007 <p> The fossil fuel industry may be responsible for a much greater share of the world 's methane emissions than previously estimated , according to new research that could intensify urgency around curbing the potent gas from oil and gas production . <p> The research , published yesterday in the journal Nature , delves into the sources of " fossil " methane emissions , or methane that comes from the Earth 's geologic formations . There are two main ways fossil methane can be released into the atmosphere -- human activities from fossil fuel production or natural processes , including the slow release of gas from mud volcanoes or undersea methane seeps . <p> Recent inventories have placed emissions from natural sources at around 40 million to 60 million metric tons of methane each year . But the new study suggests these estimates are far too high . At the very most , natural sources might contribute about 5 million tons in a given year -- and more like 1.5 million tons annually on average . <p> The researchers , led by Benjamin Hmiel of the University of Rochester , took a different approach to their estimates . Rather @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ what 's known as a " bottom-up " approach -- they instead measured the methane inside long-frozen ice samples , retrieved from a site in Greenland . <p> The ice they sampled is several hundred years old -- too old to contain any emissions from the fossil fuel industry . That means all the fossil methane preserved inside the ice comes from natural sources . They also compared these measurements with Antarctic samples from around the same time period . <p> The results suggest that researchers have been overestimating methane emissions from natural sources . <p> The new study suggests that if there 's less methane produced from natural sources , then emissions from the fossil fuel industry must be higher than previously suspected . The authors suggest that these estimates could be reasonably revised upward by about 40% . <p> If that 's the case , then the study may actually suggest an opportunity for more meaningful action to combat climate change by reducing human-caused methane emissions . Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas -- it has a much shorter lifetime in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " Placing stricter methane emission regulations on the fossil fuel industry will have the potential to reduce future global warming to a larger extent than previously thought , " said lead author Hmiel in a statement . <p> Not all scientists agree with these conclusions . Daniel Jacob , a Harvard University atmospheric chemist and methane expert , argues that the study does n't necessarily suggest that fossil fuel estimates should be higher . <p> He agrees that estimates of natural emissions were previously too high , and that the new research demonstrates they should be revised downward . But he suggests that this could mean total fossil methane emissions are lower than previously thought , not that fossil fuel emissions must be higher . <p> Aside from this critique , he says the study presents some significant findings . Jacob has worked on estimates of the global carbon budget , including the amount of total methane in the atmosphere and its possible sources . He says that previous , higher estimates of natural methane emissions had never fit well into the budget . <p> " It 's very important @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and they did this in a very convincing way , " Jacob told E&amp;E News . <p> In general , the global methane budget is often a source of confusion and debate among scientists . Atmospheric measurements suggest that methane concentrations in the air steadily increased over the 20th century , leveled off briefly around the year 2000 , and then suddenly skyrocketed in 2007 . <p> Scientists have been unable to agree on the exact source of the spike . In addition to geologic methane seeps and activity from the fossil fuel industry , methane is also produced by biological sources , like livestock , wetlands and thawing permafrost . <p> Still , in the midst of these debates , there 's recent evidence to suggest that methane emissions from the fossil fuel industry are indeed higher than previously thought . <p> Some regional studies have suggested that methane emissions from oil and gas production are actually higher than the EPA 's inventories would suggest . Other research has found that more methane could be pouring from urban environments -- potentially from leaking pipes -- than government estimates @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ methane emissions from the oil and gas supply chain could be as much as 60% higher than the levels estimated in EPA inventories . <p> Curbing methane emissions from human sources presents another opportunity for climate action , experts say -- particularly if these emissions are higher than previously suspected . <p> " I do n't want to get too hopeless on this because my data does have a positive implication : Most of the methane emissions are anthropogenic , so we have more control , " said Hmiel . " If we can reduce our emissions , it 's going to have more of an impact . " <p> Reprinted from Climatewire with permission from E&amp;E News . E&amp;E provides daily coverage of essential energy and environmental news at www.eenews.net . <p> Scientific American is part of Springer Nature , which owns or has commercial relations with thousands of scientific publications ( many of them can be found at **25;1002;TOOLONG ) . Scientific American maintains a strict policy of editorial independence in reporting developments in science to our readers .

There is no measure in the oral tradition . It 's a storytelling tradition . So you have songs and prayers and spells and stories . @@84148703 <h> Clean Energy Is Also Resilient Energy <p> After years of increasingly severe hurricane seasons in which island countries and territories in the Caribbean have lost power for weeks and even months at a time , the need for climate resilience could not be clearer . And as the Bahamas is showing , the cleanest energy sources can also be the most resilient . <p> NASSAU -- The Caribbean and its surroundings are on the front lines of climate change . The Bahamas , the archipelago that stretches over the crystal-blue waters between Florida and Cuba , have been battered in recent years by devastating hurricanes , which have increased in severity and frequency as a result of global warming . As is the case worldwide , there is an element of injustice to this . Given that the Bahamas and Caribbean countries emit relatively minuscule amounts of carbon dioxide , their residents bear very little of the blame for the climate crisis . <p> But the people of the region are now flipping the script , transforming themselves from victims of climate tragedies into global leaders in clean , secure energy . The Caribbean countries have compelling economic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they have relied on imported fossil fuels to power their economies , which means they have long had to deal with the uncertainties of world oil markets and thus significant cost fluctuations for electricity . <p> Thanks to advances in renewable energies , that economic challenge has created an opportunity . Unlike imported fossil fuels , which are subject to rising costs , the prices of solar power and other clean energy sources , along with the necessary battery storage systems , continue to fall . As these technologies have become more affordable and competitive with older , dirtier fuels , they have created a powerful incentive for island countries to move away from conventional fossil fuel-fired power plants . Moreover , this trend will only grow more pronounced from here on out , as the cost advantages of newer , cleaner energies make them increasingly attractive relative to fossil fuels . <p> For regions like the Caribbean , solar and battery storage systems do more than simply reduce the costs of electricity ; when deployed in the right way , they also improve climate resilience . As the Bahamas @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ past few years , solar- and battery-powered microgrids can provide critical services for island communities during and after severe weather events that otherwise would knock traditional energy sources offline . <p> But in order for these new energy solutions to provide real resilience , they themselves need to be able to withstand the storms , which tend to ravage power lines and disconnect communities from centralized sources of energy generation . Thus , in the case of solar , much depends on the methods used to secure solar panels to the ground and to rooftops . <p> We already know that it is possible to construct photovoltaic ( PV ) systems capable of surviving even the most severe category of hurricane . Through a collaboration between the Rocky Mountain Institute , the government of the Bahamas , and the country 's national utility , the Bahamas Power and Light Company ( BPL ) , we have developed and installed a solar parking canopy at the National Stadium in Nassau that can withstand the winds of a category-five hurricane . We have also built the country 's first category-five resilient solar @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ now focusing on designing and delivering sustainable and resilient microgrids for critical facilities on Abaco , following the destruction wrought by Hurricane Dorian in September 2019 . <h> Subscribe now <h> Subscribe today and get unlimited access to OnPoint , the Big Picture , the PS archive of more than 14,000 commentaries , and our annual magazine , for less than $2 a week . <p> SUBSCRIBE <p> As the planet continues to warm , increased moisture in the air will translate into even more severe and frequent tropical storms and hurricanes . What we saw with Dorian and Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico in 2017 is likely to become commonplace . Fortunately , as the partnership in the Bahamas shows , many of the same measures needed to build resilience are also those needed to limit greenhouse-gas ( GHG ) emissions and slow the pace of global warming . Far from requiring a tradeoff , resilient PV systems check both boxes . <p> The Caribbean and Atlantic are hardly the only regions that will need to build more resilient energy infrastructure to prevent power disruptions . Communities around the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ extreme weather , including the devastating fires in Australia , Indonesia , and the Western United States . <p> In all of these cases , clean , localized energy solutions offer unique advantages in terms of reducing emissions and keeping the lights on after a disaster . They point the way to a better future for our electricity system . By embracing the clean-energy transition , the Bahamas is setting an example for the rest of the world -- and particularly for those countries that are responsible for the overwhelming share of global GHG emissions . <h> New Comment <p> It appears that you have not yet updated your first and last name . @@84148706 <p> Two disturbing national trends -- scorched-earth politics and a failure to act boldly on the climate crisis -- came together in Oregon last week . For the fifth time in less than a year , legislators opposed to the majority party 's agenda fled instead of fulfilling their core responsibility as elected officials : to represent their constituents by casting votes in the legislative process . <p> From North Carolina to Wisconsin to Washington DC , we 've seen increasingly reckless behavior to block the will of the voters on a range of issues . In Oregon , with the anti-climate lawmakers gone , House Speaker Tina Kotek ended the legislative session , acknowledging that there was no time left to adequately consider more than one hundred pieces of legislation that were hanging in the balance . She rejected a radical proposal to allow a small minority of legislators to dictate what would be considered by the chamber . <p> Into that policy void , Oregon Governor Kate Brown committed to using the tools available to her to deliver the outcome demanded by the people of Oregon : meaningful action on climate that cuts pollution consistent with scientific @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ drive investment and innovation in clean technology , boost the state 's economic competitiveness and improve public health outcomes <p> What happened ? <p> Almost two weeks ago , 11 Senators and 21 Representatives walked out on their jobs , not only preventing climate action supported by a significant majority of Oregonians but also halting the basic functioning of government , including the passage of a budget to allow the state to operate . The walkout meant both houses of the Legislature were denied " quorum , " a Constitutional requirement that two-thirds of all members be present to hold a vote . <p> These members left a full two weeks before the Constitutional end of session , refusing to return to their taxpayer-funded jobs , halting the functioning of the legislature on myriad critical issues including measures to prepare the state for earthquakes and the coronavirus , and then at the 11th hour " offered " to come back for 12 hours to vote for bills of their choosing , effectively proposing a true tyranny of the minority . This is not the first time that an obstructionist minority has refused to do their jobs in order to block legislative action on the climate . Over the three years that they have been delaying , denying , and obstructing , Oregon could have made real progress slashing climate pollution and investing in clean energy solutions across the state , helping to lead the nation in solving the climate crisis and growing good jobs from Pendleton to Klamath Falls . <p> What 's next ? <p> Governor Brown has two main options for the immediate action on climate Oregon needs . @@84263411 <p> The South Australian coast is surrounded by a labyrinth of underwater canyons , many of them still unexplored . Last week , an international team of researchers ( and their underwater robot companion ) completed a survey of three such canyons , uncovering a hidden world of both thriving coral gardens and ash-white coral graveyards . <p> According to the expedition members , the fate of these hidden ecosystems , which sit in the immediate path of the increasingly warm water flowing out of Antarctica 's Southern Ocean , could be a preview of how farther-flung ocean life will react to ongoing global warming . <p> " This has global implications given these waters originate from around Antarctica and feed all of the major oceans and regulate our climate system , " expedition member Malcolm McCulloch , of the University of Western Australia , said in a statement . <p> In their recent voyage , McCulloch and his colleagues aboard the research vessel R/V Falkor ( named for the luck dragon of NeverEnding Story fame ) explored the depths of three canyons on the South Australia coast -- Bremer , Leeuwin and Perth canyons -- descending for the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the dark depths roughly 2.5 miles ( 4,000 meters ) below the surface . <p> Beyond the obvious reason for such exploration ( hidden worlds are awesome ) , scientists are interested in these submarine crannies because they sit on the front lines of oceanic climate change . Facing the Southern Ocean -- the ocean that surrounds Antarctica and connects the Atlantic , Pacific and Indian oceans with its clockwise-flowing current -- these canyons are some of the first ecosystems on Earth to encounter the warming waters surging out of Antarctica 's ocean . <p> Thanks to a mechanism called the Antarctic convergence ( in which cold water flowing north clashes with warmer , south-flowing water ) , the currents leaving the Southern Ocean are remarkably rich in nutrients . That makes the submarine canyons of South Australia a hotspot for migrating animals . Bremer Canyon , for example , is home to the Southern Hemisphere 's largest seasonal gathering of killer whales and often hosts traveling sharks , dolphins , squids and birds , the researchers said . <p> During their latest expedition , the crew of the Falkor @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Each spot hosted lush gardens of coral , rich with marine life and bursting with color . However , each canyon ( especially Leeuwin ) also contained extensive pockets of dead and fossilized coral . According to the researchers , these corals bear the record of both recent , anthropogenic ocean warming , as well as longer-term changes to the world 's climate . It 's not clear yet what killed the coral in a given canyon , but researchers will begin answering that question as soon as Falkor returns to land . <p> This voyage was funded by the nonprofit Schmidt Ocean Institute , and the team 's newest research has yet to appear in a peer-reviewed journal . <p> With impressive cutaway illustrations that show how things function , and mindblowing photography of the world 's most inspiring spectacles , How It Works represents the pinnacle of engaging , factual fun for a mainstream audience keen to keep up with the latest tech and the most impressive phenomena on the planet and beyond . He was under hospice care @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ During his six-decade career , the charismatic , husky-voiced singer sold more than 100 million albums worldwide , won three Grammy Awards and was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame . He also published several photography books , donated time and money to philanthropic causes , appeared in a number of made-for-television movies and launched an eponymous restaurant chain . <p> Kenneth Donald Rogers ( called " Kenneth Ray " by his family members ) was born in Houston on Aug. 21 , 1938 . The fourth of Edward and Lucille 's eight children , Rogers grew up in the San Felipe Courts housing project and was the first person in his family to receive a high school diploma . <p> " As early as grade school , I began to see music and singing as a respite from all the awkwardness and embarrassment of growing up poor , shy and often an outsider , " Rogers wrote in his 2012 book , " Luck or Something Like It : A Memoir . " <p> He entered his first talent contest when he was 10 years old . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ grand prize : a half-gallon of vanilla ice cream and a meeting with country star Eddy Arnold . <p> In high school , he formed a vocal group called the Scholars . They cut a few forgettable tracks for L.A. label Imperial Records , then went their separate ways . As a solo artist , Kenneth Rogers ( who 'd soon change his stage name to Kenny ) recorded a song called " That Crazy Feeling , " which was released on Carlton Records . At age 19 , he performed the teen-dream ballad on " American Bandstand . " <p> In 1959 , jazz pianist Bobby Doyle heard Rogers play at a club and asked him to join the Bobby Doyle Three as a bassist and harmony singer . Rogers was n't a bass player but signed on anyway . " The band released it as its second single -- the first with Rogers singing lead . The psychedelic-sounding song went to No. 5 on the charts and , as Rogers wrote in " Luck or Something Like It , " it gave the band " street cred during ... a time of massive social change , when music was expected to be edgy and , in many cases , drug related .
